name: Handy v. Jones
court: Ninth Circuit (from the District of Alaska)
citation: No. 25-5105 (9th Cir. Sept. 15, 2026) (reporter citation not yet available in the sources read)
topic: Fourth Amendment deadly force; armed domestic violence suspect advancing on officers with a shotgun while refusing commands; qualified immunity granted on a motion to dismiss; no requirement that the gun be pointed at officers
summary: Anchorage officers responding to reports that a man had assaulted his girlfriend, that shots had been heard, and that he was waiting outside with a shotgun ordered him out of his apartment. He emerged with the shotgun, refused repeated commands to drop it, cursed at the officers, and walked toward them waving the gun over his head; four officers shot him nine times as he stepped off the curb. The district court denied qualified immunity on a motion to dismiss. The Ninth Circuit vacated and directed entry of qualified immunity, holding that on the complaint and the incorporated video the man posed an immediate threat, that an officer need not wait for a suspect to point a gun at him before firing, and that no case clearly established otherwise. It is taught for the totality of the circumstances approach to an armed, noncompliant, advancing suspect after Barnes v. Felix.
coverage: The full opinion by Judge Callahan, joined by Judges Bea and Bumatay, including the staff summary and all footnotes, was read from https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2026/09/15/25-5105.pdf. The slip opinion is headed No. 25-5105, D.C. No. 3:24-cv-00178-SLG, argued and submitted August 10, 2026 in Anchorage, filed September 15, 2026, and marked for publication.
No reporter citation was available in the sources read. The brief cites the docket and filing date.

The opinion arose on an interlocutory appeal from the denial of a motion to dismiss. The court reviewed the complaint together with a department produced video the complaint incorporated by reference, viewing ambiguities in the plaintiffs' favor. The video itself was not viewed for this brief; its contents are described only as the court described them.

The cases discussed by the court (George v. Morris, Estate of Lopez v. Gelhaus, Nehad v. Browder, Napouk v. Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, Blanford v. Sacramento County, Hughes v. Kisela, Hayes v. County of San Diego, Curnow v. Ridgecrest Police) were not read; they are described as the Handy court described them.
No petition for rehearing or certiorari was checked. The opinion is recent and its subsequent history is unknown to this brief.
facts:
The facts are as the Ninth Circuit stated them from the complaint and the video the complaint incorporated, viewed in the plaintiffs' favor. Late on the night of May 13, 2024, a neighbor called 911 several times to report a disturbance in Kristopher Handy's Anchorage apartment between Handy and his girlfriend. She reported hearing the woman screaming for him to stop, a loud thud against the wall, and later what sounded like two shots inside the house. She told the dispatcher that Handy, appearing very agitated, was standing at the end of the driveway holding a shotgun, waiting for the police to come around the corner. The complaint stated that this information was conveyed to the multiple officers who responded.

The officers announced their presence and directed Handy to come out of the apartment. He exited carrying his shotgun. Officers instructed him multiple times to put his hands in the air and drop the gun; each time he refused. The video confirmed that as he walked toward the officers in the parking lot he waved the shotgun over his head and, when ordered to put his hands up, cursed at them. As Handy stepped off the curb onto the parking area, four officers shot him nine times, killing him.

Handy's relatives sued the four officers under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, alleging excessive force under the Fourth Amendment and deprivation of their right to familial association. The officers moved to dismiss on qualified immunity. The district court denied the motion. It reasoned that once Handy came out of the apartment he was no longer an immediate threat to the victim, that he was walking at a casual pace rather than charging, that the neighbor never saw him raise the gun, that not all the officers fired, that the officers had warned him only that a dog would be used if he did not come out and had not warned that deadly force would be used if he did not drop the gun, and that Ninth Circuit cases had allowed a factfinder to conclude that officers were not in danger when a suspect held a weapon at his side without threatening movement. It declined to consider Napouk v. Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department because that case was decided after the shooting. The officers appealed.
holding:
Vacated and remanded with directions to enter an order granting the officers qualified immunity. Judge Callahan wrote for the panel.

Jurisdiction. An order denying qualified immunity is immediately appealable, and it did not matter that the ruling came on a motion to dismiss rather than summary judgment; the court reviewed the complaint and the incorporated video in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs, and the plaintiffs did not claim they were denied an opportunity to present material.

The district court applied the wrong test. The question is not whether a reasonable factfinder could find that Handy did not pose an immediate threat, but whether it would be objectively reasonable for the officer to believe that the amount of force employed was required by the situation he confronted (Napouk, quoting Wilkins v. City of Oakland). Reasonableness is judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene allowing for split second judgments, and a determination of reasonableness on a motion to dismiss or for summary judgment does not mean the officer could not have taken some other action. Under Scott v. Harris, where video is in the record a court views the facts in the light depicted by the video rather than adopting a version blatantly contradicted by it.

The Graham factors. First, the officers reasonably believed Handy may have committed a violent crime: he was reported to have assaulted his girlfriend with a shotgun present and to have waited for the officers armed with the shotgun. Second, a reasonable officer could think he was resisting arrest when he refused repeated commands to drop the weapon and instead waved it over his head and cursed. Third, and most importantly, the video showed that Handy posed an immediate threat to the officers' safety: he was belligerently waving a shotgun as he continued to advance toward them. None of the factors the district court cited reduced his dangerousness. Although he did not point the shotgun at the officers, he could have fired it from the hip instantly. His exit may have reduced the threat to his girlfriend but he continued to threaten the officers. His casual pace did not matter because he remained armed, agitated, and capable of immediately firing. That some officers did not fire did not mean he was not an immediate threat.

The district court's cases. George v. Morris involved a husband not suspected of a crime who had shown no animosity to police, did not move toward them, and never moved his gun from its position at his side. Lopez involved a minor with a toy rifle who was not suspected of a crime, was not advancing, and turned only in response to the officer's call. Nehad involved a misdemeanor call, a man armed at most with a knife, and an officer who shot before determining whether there was a threat. Hughes v. Kisela, reversed by the Supreme Court, Hayes, and Curnow were likewise distinguishable; none suggests an officer must wait to be targeted before shooting in self defense.

Barnes and the totality of the circumstances. The court said the Supreme Court in Barnes v. Felix rejected a focus on the moment of threat in favor of a totality of the circumstances analysis with no time limit, in which earlier facts bear on how a reasonable officer would understand later ones. Here the facts that Handy was suspected of assaulting his girlfriend, had awaited the officers armed with a shotgun, had refused orders to drop it, was advancing, was belligerent, and could fire from the hip together showed he was dangerous regardless of where the shotgun was pointed. The Ninth Circuit had applied the same approach in Napouk, affirming immunity for officers who shot a man who came within nine feet armed with a machete or slim jim, and in Blanford, affirming immunity for officers who shot a sword carrying man who ignored commands and tried to enter a home; the court said neither of those suspects posed a threat as immediate as Handy's. Other circuits agree that an armed, belligerent suspect may pose an immediate threat without pointing the gun (Knibbs, Fourth Circuit; Estate of Rahim, First Circuit; Garczynski, Eleventh Circuit).

Holding. Viewing the totality of the circumstances in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs, Handy posed a lethal threat and the officers did not violate the Constitution by shooting him. Alternatively, even if a violation could be shown, no case placed the unlawfulness of their conduct beyond debate: none of the district court's cases suggests that an officer facing an armed individual suspected of a violent crime must hold fire until the individual actually aims the gun at the officer, a proposition the court said was implicitly rejected in Barnes, Napouk, and Blanford.
notDecided:
Whether a deadly force warning was required. The district court faulted the officers for warning only about the dog and not about deadly force; the Ninth Circuit's analysis did not treat the absence of a deadly force warning as changing the result on these facts, but it did not announce a rule about warnings.

The familial association claim as a separate matter. The court's disposition directed entry of qualified immunity on the complaint; it analyzed the Fourth Amendment question and did not separately discuss the Fourteenth Amendment standard.

Whether the officers' tactics before the shooting, including ordering Handy out of the apartment with a dog warning, were sound. The court addressed only whether the shooting was reasonable in light of all the circumstances.

How much of the video was incorporated into the complaint. The parties disagreed; the court noted the disagreement and relied on the undisputed point that the officers had been informed of Handy's reported actions and threats.

Any state law claim. None is discussed.
inPractice:
Handy is the Ninth Circuit applying Barnes v. Felix to the situation officers fear most: an armed, angry, noncompliant person walking toward them. The court's answer is that an officer does not have to wait for the gun to come up. When the totality of the circumstances shows that the person is suspected of a violent crime, was reported to be waiting for police with a firearm, refuses repeated commands to drop it, curses at officers, and keeps coming while waving the weapon, the person is an immediate threat regardless of where the muzzle is pointed, because a shotgun can be fired from the hip in an instant.

The court also corrected the district court's framing in a way that matters to officers. The question is not whether a jury could imagine the person was not a threat, or whether the officer could have done something else. It is whether a reasonable officer on the scene could believe the force used was required. Where there is video, courts look at what the video shows. Officers should understand that the facts that protected these officers were documented: the 911 reports relayed to them, their repeated commands, the refusal, the waving of the gun, and the advance.

The counterexamples the court distinguished are just as instructive. George: a man with a gun at his side, not suspected of a crime, not advancing, possibly unaware police were there. Lopez: a boy with a toy rifle who turned when called. Nehad: a misdemeanor call, a possible knife, and a shot fired before any assessment. In each the court had let a jury decide. The difference in Handy was the combination of a reported violent crime, an actual firearm, refusal of commands, belligerence, and movement toward the officers.

Dr. Sowards teaches Handy with Barnes as the current totality of the circumstances framework and with Hernandez for contrast on when the justification ends. The lesson is to know and be able to articulate every fact that bears on the threat, not just the position of the weapon.
trainIt:
Teach the threat assessment as a list of facts, not a single cue. The district court focused on where the shotgun was pointed and how fast Handy walked. The Ninth Circuit listed the facts a reasonable officer would weigh together: the reported assault, the reported shots, the report that he was waiting for police with the gun, the refusal of repeated commands, the cursing, the waving of the weapon, the advance, and the ability to fire from the hip. Have students build that list in a scenario and articulate it in the order they learned each fact. This is what Barnes means by the totality of the circumstances.

Teach the domestic violence call context. The court quoted the rule that officers responding to domestic abuse calls understand that violence may be lurking and explode with little warning. The 911 information in Handy came from a neighbor and was relayed by dispatch; train students to listen for and record what dispatch tells them, because those facts become part of the reasonableness analysis.

Teach commands and warnings. The officers repeatedly ordered Handy to put his hands up and drop the gun, and he refused. The district court faulted the absence of a specific deadly force warning. The Ninth Circuit did not require one on these facts, but Garner and Ninth Circuit cases treat feasible warnings as relevant. Train students to give a clear, specific warning when time permits and to document that it was given and refused.

Teach the contrast cases. Run George, Lopez, and Nehad as scenarios alongside Handy and have students explain why the court sent those to a jury and not this one. The difference is not the presence of a weapon; it is the crime, the noncompliance, the belligerence, and the movement toward officers.

Teach the limit from Hernandez: once the threat is down and not getting up, the justification must be reassessed. Handy addresses the decision to fire, not when to stop.

applications.title: No duty to wait for the gun to come up
applications.body: An armed suspect reported to have committed a violent crime, who refuses repeated commands to drop the weapon and advances while waving it and cursing, poses an immediate threat regardless of where the gun is pointed, because it can be fired instantly from the hip.

applications.title: The right question
applications.body: The test is whether a reasonable officer could believe the force used was required by the situation, judged from the scene and allowing for split second judgments, not whether a factfinder could imagine the suspect was not a threat or whether some other action was possible.

applications.title: Totality, as Barnes requires
applications.body: The court listed every earlier fact known to the officers, the reported assault, the shots heard, the report that he was waiting with a shotgun, and the refusals, and held that together they showed danger regardless of the muzzle's direction.

applications.title: Why the contrast cases went to a jury
applications.body: A man with a gun at his side who is not suspected of a crime and not advancing, a boy with a toy rifle who turns when called, or a possible knife on a misdemeanor call are different. The combination of crime, firearm, noncompliance, belligerence, and advance made Handy's case different.

applications.title: Video shows what it shows
applications.body: Where video is in the record, a court views the facts as the video depicts them. The officers' commands, Handy's refusals, and his advance were on video. Document and preserve the recording of every such encounter.

quiz.q: What did the Ninth Circuit identify as the district court's error in framing the qualified immunity question in Handy v. Jones?
options: It asked whether a reasonable factfinder could find Handy was not a threat, rather than whether a reasonable officer could believe the force used was required by the situation
It required a deadly force warning
quiz.teach: The court said reasonableness is judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene allowing for split second judgments, and that a finding of reasonableness does not mean the officer could not have taken some other action.

quiz.q: Did the court require that Handy point the shotgun at the officers before deadly force could be reasonable?
options: Yes, pointing the weapon is always required
No; the court held that an armed, belligerent suspect advancing after refusing commands posed an immediate threat regardless of where the gun was pointed, because he could fire from the hip
Yes, unless the officers had cover
The court did not address the question
quiz.teach: The court relied on Barnes v. Felix, Napouk, and Blanford and on decisions from other circuits holding that an officer need not wait to be targeted before shooting in self defense.

quiz.q: How did the court distinguish George v. Morris, where it had let a jury decide whether shooting an armed man was reasonable?
options: In George the man was not suspected of a crime, showed no animosity to police, did not move toward them, and never moved his gun from his side
George was decided after the shooting
quiz.teach: The court said Handy, an armed adult suspected of a violent crime who advanced in a belligerent manner while refusing commands, posed a kind of immediate danger that the suspects in George, Lopez, and Nehad did not.
